content.title: FOOD FACTS THAT SOUND MADE UP BUT AREN'T
facts: **Cashews** are never sold in their shells to consumers — the shell contains a resin so caustic it's chemically related to poison ivy, and roasting is required just to make them safe to touch.

**Nutmeg** contains a natural compound called myristicin that, in large enough doses, is genuinely hallucinogenic and toxic — the amount in your pumpkin pie is nowhere near it, but a few whole teaspoons could send you to the ER.
**Carrots** were originally purple, not orange — the orange variety was bred in the Netherlands centuries ago, partly as a tribute to the royal House of Orange.

**Pineapple** contains an enzyme called bromelain that actually digests proteins — which is why it can literally start breaking down the flesh in your mouth, making your tongue feel raw after too much.
**Almonds** are technically not nuts at all — they're seeds found inside the fruit of the almond tree, which looks similar to a peach.
**Strawberries** aren't berries, but bananas botanically are — the seeds-on-the-outside fruit you eat for breakfast fails the technical definition that a real berry has to meet.
**Chili peppers** trigger the exact same pain receptor in your mouth that responds to actual heat — your brain can't tell the difference between spicy food and a hot stove.
**Apples** float in water because they're roughly 25% air by volume — that trapped air is also why bobbing for apples actually works.

content.caption:
The cashew fact still gets people every time — cashews grow attached to the bottom of a cashew apple, encased in a shell filled with a resin called urushiol, the same irritant found in poison ivy, which is exactly why you never see them sold raw and unshelled. Nutmeg sounds harmless because it's just a baking spice, but myristicin is a real psychoactive compound that your liver has to work hard to metabolize — home bakers have accidentally poisoned themselves trying to get "high" off it, which is a good reminder that dose is everything in nutrition. And pineapple's bromelain enzyme is so effective at breaking down protein that it's actually used commercially as a meat tenderizer — your saliva just happens to be made of protein too, which is why pineapple seems to "fight back." Food chemistry is wild once you actually look into it.
